The Second Classification of the Arabian Shield

Dr. Ahmad Redaa

2026-02-18

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lecture, students should be able to:

  • Explain the historical rationale for the 2nd classification (central–northern Shield focus).
  • Describe the two-cycle tectonic framework: Assir Cycle + Najd Cycle.
  • Summarize each Group/Formation (lithology, environment, tectonic meaning, age ranges).
  • Critically evaluate the limitations of the classification.
  • Compare the 1st classification, 2nd classification, and modern terrane-based models.

Historical context

  • The 2nd classification is based on investigations in the central and northern Arabian Shield (Delfour, 1982).
  • Key field observation: gneissic granitic belts separated by belts of ophiolites and volcanic–volcaniclastic rocks.
  • Interpretation: gneissic belts represent an older crustal nucleus that formed and cratonized prior to the Najd tectonism, then was reworked during Najd collision/accretion.

The conceptual shift vs 1st classification

  • 1st classification: essentially a single long tectono-stratigraphic evolution (Hijaz Cycle).
  • 2nd classification: Arabian Shield evolved through two successive tectonic cycles:
    • Assir Tectonic Cycle (older “continental basement” stage)
    • Najd Tectonic Cycle (880–610 Ma; major accretion, sedimentation, deformation)

Conceptual tectonic model (2nd classification)

Two-cycle framework

Assir Cycle (≥1000–900 Ma; poorly exposed/recognized)
- Forms early continental crust (gneiss + schist belts).
- Later tectonic events obscure early structures; final stages inferred ~1000–900 Ma.

Najd Cycle (880–610 Ma; ~270 Ma duration)
- Dominant observable Shield evolution: sedimentation + volcanism + ophiolite emplacement + plutonism + deformation.
- Correlated with Pan-African activity in the Nubian Shield.

Assir Tectonic Cycle: main components (overview)

  • Old Basement: gneissic belts (Sawdah, Rakhamah) intruded/reworked by younger Najd plutons.
  • Al Hajal Group: part of old basement but locally preserves original characteristics better.
  • Al Ghorabah (Rhaharabah) layered complexes: basic–ultrabasic intrusions near the Assir/Najd boundary and throughout Najd evolution (800–700 Ma typical).

Old Basement: belts and lithology

Sawdah Belt

  • Foliated diorite–quartz diorite with plagioclase, hornblende, biotite.
  • Retrograde metamorphism to chlorite–epidote schists; roof pendants/inclusions (quartzite, silicic volcanics), migmatites.

Rakhamah Belt

  • Gneissic granite (K-feldspar, plagioclase, biotite ± muscovite).
  • Contains inclusions of biotite gneiss/schist; heterogeneous granodiorite bodies.

Note: Rb/Sr ages often not older than ~940 Ma due to Najd reworking/rejuvenation.

Al Hajal Group (Assir Cycle remnants)

  • Occurs south of Halaban: belt between an ophiolite belt (east) and old basement (west).
  • Lithology: amphibolite gneiss layers; quartz–oligoclase–hornblende–biotite gneiss; calcareous schist, marble, quartzite.
  • Structure/metamorphism: isoclinal tight folding; amphibolite facies; interpreted as originally sedimentary protoliths.
  • Reported resemblance/correlation problems with Hali Schist and old basement rocks (difficult to differentiate).

Al Ghorabah layered complexes (basic–ultrabasic)

  • Funnel-shaped, layered intrusions cutting: Old Basement, Al Hajal Group, Hulayfah Group.
  • Composition: gabbro + anorthosite ± serpentinite; generally rigid/massive; limited metamorphism except margins.
  • Crosscut by granite/dacite/rhyolite/aplite dikes.
  • Typical ages: ~800–700 Ma; interpreted as upper mantle-derived intrusions into evolving crust during Najd cycle.

Najd Tectonic Cycle: overview (880–610 Ma)

  • Major period of Shield evolution (~270 Ma).
  • Includes: deposition of multiple sedimentary/volcanic groups, ophiolite emplacement, alternating deformation/metamorphism, and varied plutonism.
  • Comparable to Pan-African period in the Nubian Shield.

Najd Cycle: stratigraphic architecture

  1. Urd Group (Abt + Ar Ridayniyah; overlain by Hulayfah)
  2. Hulayfah Group (Afnah + Nugrah; arc volcanics & volcaniclastics)
  3. Contemporaneous basin groups (regional equivalents):
    • Murdamah, Shammar (central/north)
    • Furayh, Hadiyah (western/northwestern)
    • Al Ays (NW basin; debated correlations)
  4. Jibalah Group (late, least metamorphosed; associated with Najd faulting)

Ophiolites in the 2nd classification

  • Delfour annexed ophiolitic rocks to Urd Group.
  • The document itself notes this is not accepted stratigraphically:
    • Ophiolites are tectonically emplaced slices, not conformable layered successions.
  • Many belts are dismembered (Penrose-style ophiolite concept referenced).

Urd Group: Abt + Ar Ridayniyah (summary)

  • Layered successions unconformably overlying ophiolites in the east Shield.
  • Correlated conceptually with Baish + Bahah in SW Shield.

Ar Ridayniyah Formation (Urd Group)

  • Location: ~35 km SE of Ad Dawadimi; adjacent to ophiolite belts.
  • Lithology: calcareous schist, marble, amphibolite, quartzite; interpreted from dolomite/limestone + arenaceous/pelitic protoliths.
  • Environment: shallow marine, shoreline facies relative to Abt basin; rapid facies change.
  • Complex relations: some basalts within may relate to ophiolite; melange-like gabbro bodies; possible ocean-floor sediments interlayered with basalt.
  • Intrusions: basic/acidic dikes; adamellite sills.

Abt Formation (Urd Group)

  • Deposited in a N–S trending basin (~250 × 70 km) at far eastern Shield.
  • Very thick pelitic schist–phyllite succession (up to ~10 km).
  • Protoliths: greywacke, siltstone, volcanic shale ± basic volcanic flows; conglomerate locally (e.g., base near Jabal Tays).
  • Metamorphism increases near intrusions (biotite schist → gneiss; garnet near contacts = contact effects).

Tuluhah Orogeny (affecting Urd Group)

  • Abt + Ar Ridayniyah metamorphosed to greenschist facies; folded at least twice.
  • Intrusions: diabase, granite, aplite, adamellite; plus biotite granite/granodiorite with contact halos.

Hulayfah Group: overview

  • Occurs as N–S trending belts in central/northern Shield.
  • Dominant lithologies: volcanic flows + volcaniclastics + epiclastic sediments, with marble and chert.
  • Metamorphism/structure: regional greenschist facies; folding and faulting; intruded by calc-alkaline granitic to dioritic bodies.
  • Volcanism: calc-alkaline dacite and andesite dominant; basalt and rhyolite also present.
  • Subdivided into Afnah (lower) and Nugrah (upper) formations.

Afnah Formation (Hulayfah Group)

  • Well exposed succession (Jabal Tin/Twin/Afnah).
  • Lower: conglomerate + carbonates + greywacke + volcanic sandstone + rhyolite tuff.
  • Upper: interbedded basalt + andesite flows with volcaniclastics.
  • Thickness: ~6000–7000 m near Musayn’ah prospect; strong lateral/vertical facies changes.
  • Geochemistry: calc-alkaline basalt/andesite → active margin / moderate to immature island-arc affinity.

Nugrah Formation (Hulayfah Group)

  • Lower: felsic volcanics (rhyolite crystal tuff, rhyolitic tuff, breccia) ± andesite layers; conformably over Afnah.
  • Transitional contact may be gradational (200–300 m interbedded andesite+rhyolite).
  • Economic geology: hosts polymetallic VMS deposits associated with acidic volcanics.
  • Middle “mine zone”: dolomitic lenses + acidic graphitic schist; marble indicates volcanic quiescence; chert; primary structures (cross-bedding, graded bedding).
  • Upper: conglomerate with rhyolite pebbles ± quartz; ignimbrite; coarse rhyolite tuff; thin-bedded tuffs.

Ar Ragabah Orogeny (affecting Hulayfah Group)

  • Regional greenschist metamorphism + deformation.
  • Local tight isoclinal folding; unconformable relations (Shammar or Murdamah may overlie Hulayfah).
  • Intrusions: predominantly calc-alkaline, diorite → granite; sharp contacts, contact metamorphism, locally skarn.
  • Age range (Rb–Sr): ~800–690 Ma.

Al Ays Group (NW basin; correlation issues)

  • Basin NW of Al Madinah.
  • Delfour: contemporaneous with Murdamah + Shammar (thus younger than Hulayfah).
  • Other work cited: correlation with Ablah; Rb/Sr on silica tuff gives ~743–725 Ma; tonalite pluton (U–Pb zircon) ~725 Ma → suggests older than Murdamah and possibly correlates with Halaban/Hulayfah.
  • Lithology: thick volcanic sediments + flows + volcaniclastics; locally bimodal; conglomerate/silt/mud abundant; variable environments shallow→deep; volcanic centers east/south.
  • Intrusions: layered basic bodies (Al Ghorabah-like) + diorite, granodiorite, adamellite.
  • Deformation: folding/faulting; regional metamorphism to schists obscuring original features.

Murdamah Group (Najd Cycle basin fill)

  • Extensive distribution; in central/north forms a N–S basin near Afif (~600 km long, ~50 km wide; up to ~10 km thickness).
  • Shallow-water elastic sediments; subdivided into four formations (base→top): Hibshi, Faridah, Zeidi, Hadiyah.

Hibshi Formation (Murdamah)

  • Thick polygenic conglomerates (thicker northward); plus fine sandstone, greywacke, rhyolite tuffs.
  • Unconformably overlies intrusions linked to Hulayfah Group; pebbles derived from those intrusions + andesite/rhyolite pebbles from Hulayfah.
  • Thickness ~7000 m.

Faridah Formation (Murdamah)

  • Carbonate-rich margins (marble + dolomite; thickest in eastern margin: Jabal Faridah/Damkh).
  • Variegated marble (grey dominant); thin shale, elastic limestone, calcareous conglomerate interbeds.
  • Interpreted as unstable basin with pauses; stromatolites and laminations common.

Zeidi Formation (Murdamah)

  • Basin-wide shallow-water sandstone–siltstone–shale.
  • Abundant sedimentary structures: cross-lamination, cross-bedding, graded bedding, ripple marks, etc.
  • Polymictic conglomerates indicate unstable basin + intense erosion.
  • Local andesite flows + ignimbrite + welded rhyolite breccia present.

Hadiyah Formation (Murdamah)

  • Upper Murdamah in north; unconformably overlies Al Ays.
  • Thick clastics (shale, slate, sandstone, conglomerate) derived from diverse volcanics; some marble + quartzite.
  • Type locality near ruined Hadiyah railway station N of Al Madinah; ~200 m thick; shallow-water indicators common.

Furayh Group (transitional)

  • SW of Al Madinah.
  • Volcanic + sedimentary succession in near-equal proportions.
  • Transitional between Murdamah (clastic) and Shammar (volcanic).

Shammar Group (late felsic volcanism)

  • Felsic volcanic suite (rhyolite/ignimbrite/pyroclastics), detailed elsewhere but retained here as a Najd-cycle unit.
  • Relationships: may overlie Hulayfah unconformably in some belts.

Late Najd: Ar Rimmah Orogeny (690–610 Ma)

  • Correlates with Bishah Orogeny of the 1st classification.
  • Regional deformation + greenschist metamorphism affecting Murdamah, Shammar, Furayh.
  • Intrusions: diorite to granite; granites often elliptical or ring granites; alkalic to peralkalic.
  • Duration ~80 Ma (from intrusive ages).

Summary table: Groups & formations (2nd classification)

[A. M. S. Al-Shanti, “Geology of the Arabian Shield of Saudi Arabia,” Scientific Publishing Center, King Abdulaziz University, 2009, p.190.]

Limitations of the 2nd classification

  1. Ophiolites treated as stratigraphic units
    • Ophiolite belts are tectonic slices; inclusion within Urd stratigraphy is stratigraphically problematic.
  2. Isotopic “rejuvenation” of basement
    • Basement ages may be reset during Najd tectonism; true pre-Najd ages obscured.
  3. Two-cycle oversimplification
    • Real accretionary histories may involve multiple diachronous arcs/collisions not resolved here.
  4. Limited terrane and suture resolution
    • Recognizes basement vs Najd belts, but does not fully implement modern terrane boundary logic.

Comparison: 1st vs 2nd vs modern models

1st classification (Hijaz cycle focus)

  • Emphasizes progressive stratigraphic/chemical evolution through episodes and orogenies.
  • Does not explicitly require an older continental basement.

2nd classification (Assir + Najd)

  • Introduces older continental basement belts (Assir Cycle) and major Najd cycle.
  • Better integrates ophiolite belts (even if stratigraphically debated).
  • Correlates Najd with Pan-African.

Modern tectonic models

  • Treat the Shield as an accretionary collage of terranes:
    • discrete arcs, sutures, ophiolite-bearing belts, transcurrent systems
  • Use high-precision geochronology/isotopes to resolve diachronous evolution.
